lines: Tuesday, 12 May 2026
ARBITRATOR:  Good morning, and welcome to the first day of
hearing on DIAC arbitration case 240007.
Assuming we have a timetable with us.
Thank you for, first of all, the parties for
convening together and facilitating things for this
hearing and the coming days for the hearing.
I think we need to start the hearing saying that me
as a sole tribunal of the case, I'll try to accommodate
all parties' requests, and what they require to prove
their parts of the case.  What I am urging all the
parties here, that is try to use the maximum to the
benefit of your cases for the two parties.  Just go
directly to your points.  If there is anything I have
a question, I might ask the counsels of both parties.
Otherwise we need just to be efficient on our
proceeding.
I know everybody is too busy, everybody work hard,
but again, we need just to accommodate everyone also, to
give them the comfort that we will listen to everyone's
point of view.
Any housekeeping matters, both counsels, you need to
address it before we start the hearing?
MS BEJOY:  None from my side.
MR LIXENBURG:  No, thank you very much.
ARBITRATOR:  I'm assuming the attendance sheets will be
here.
MS BEJOY:  Yes.
ARBITRATOR:  Both parties?  Okay.
Let's start: claimant, please, start your opening.
MS BEJOY:  Thank you very much, arbitrator.
Opening submission by MS BEJOY
MS BEJOY:  Good morning, everyone.  Myself, Asha Bejoy,
along with me I have my four colleagues, Jerome Jose,
Aeron and then we have the client representative,
Mr Ayad, and Ms Pzifer, (^chk name) and we also have
Mr Mohammed^sp    .
The claimants in this case, number 240007, is two
corporate entities and Mr Ayad.  The corporate entities
are Pacific Real Estate Development LLC, and Al Turfa
Building Contracting LLC.
Today, as a road map for my presentation, I will be
following the below heads.
I will take about 10 minutes to give a brief
introduction on the parties and their respective
positions.  I will then deal with one or two preliminary
issues, followed by introducing key background facts
which are important and must be understood.
Then I would be moving on to the grounds of
termination taken by the respondents, which is one of
their main grounds, and its maintainability, followed by
highlighting the claimants' monetary claims and its
maintainability.
I will then move on to the segment of who the
witnesses are and what sort of evidence they will be
introducing.  Finally, I will be concluding on what
reliefs the claimants are looking for in this
proceeding.
With your kind permission, arbitrator, may I proceed
to the introduction part of my presentation?
ARBITRATOR:  Please.
MS BEJOY:  Thank you.
So for the purposes of today's discussion I would
like the facts to be kept very brief.  In short, the
claimants have filed this claim seeking relief for
wrongful termination of their joint venture arrangement
with the respondent which was for the development of
a 300-key Yotel hotel project in Palm Jumeirah.
A few things to keep in mind.
There are three contracts which are underlying this
transaction.
The first is the memorandum of understanding,
followed by two documents, one is an earn-out agreement,
and there is another document which is a design and
build contract which talks about the
construction-related obligations of the parties.
The chronology is we have the MOU some time
in October 2015, followed by the two definitive
agreements signed three months later in February 2016.
What is claimants' case?  In simple terms, claimant
is alleging that the termination of the contracts, the
definitive agreements, meaning the earn-out agreement,
and the design and build contract, is wrongful.
And why do they say so?  That we will definitely
look into in subsequent part of my presentation.  What
are they seeking for?  In broad terms, they are asking
for monetary claims falling under the heads of: loss of
profit, undue enrichment.  There is also a claim that
their IP has been misappropriated.  Also dues in respect
of works that they have already performed.
Then there is also a claim for loss of commercial
opportunity because of their time and effort spent in
this particular project.
On top of that, they would also like to make
a claimant for interest.  Last but not least, legal and
arbitration costs that they had to incur to file this
arbitration claim.  These reliefs are very well-secured
in the claimants' statement of claim and the reply.
Of course, the reliefs got fine-tuned in reply
because when we filed a statement of claim, we did not
have much visibility on many of the aspects of the
dispute.  Much of it came to light in the disclosure
stage and the subsequent evidence stage which
necessitated us to modify our relief in our reply.
So my submission to the learned arbitrator is
because it is forming a part of the pleading, it may be
treated as part and parcel of the claim, and the
claimants would like to pursue its claim as recorded in
the statement of reply.
Now, what is the respondents' case?
Respondents hold the view that they have every right
to terminate the contracts and the termination is within
their rights.  Why?  Because essentially they have taken
three grounds.  One, failure to comply with obligations
regarding design compliance.  Failure to comply with
obligations regarding consultants and employees.  And
thirdly, failure to comply with obligations regarding
funding.
Respondents' primary position is that the
respondents have validly terminated the contracts.  What
we have to bear in mind is that we have a termination
letter that essentially terminates both documents.  And
which is dated 18 January 2018 -- sorry, the date of the
termination is, yes, 18 January 2018.
So it is their position that they have validly
terminated this contract under clause 15.2 after giving
a notice of correct under clause 15.2 of the design and
build contract, under 3.4 of the earn-out agreement.
The claimants, according to them, are not entitled
to any earned value.  This has been reflected in the
opening submission, plus all of their experts'
conclusion lead -- it is their position that there is no
earned value.  Why do they say so?  Although there has
been findings from a joint expert that close to 800/900K
is something that the parties have invested worth time
on designing.  They have come to the conclusion that
there is a liquidated damages entitlement, plus there is
also money that they had to incur to get the designs
corrected through a third party consultant.
Therefore, once we deduct the liquidated damages and
the third party consultant's fee, there is absolutely
nothing that is due to the claimant.  That's their
position.
And the respondents are seeking a dismissal of the
claimants' claim, award of counterclaim to the extent of
16 million, and an order for the claimants to pay all
costs and interests.
So that is a brief introduction on both parties'
position and the underlying dispute.
I would now like to move on to the preliminary
issues that I would like to deal with before moving into
the merits of the dispute.
There are essentially two preliminary issues.
Issue 1, preliminary issue 1, is regarding
jurisdiction.  So the respondents have taken a view
that, as I told, there are two documents, the earn-out
agreement, and the design and build contract.  So the
respondents, in their submission, have taken the view
that the arbitrator cannot look into the legality of the
termination under the design and build contract because
this particular arbitration is initiated under the
arbitration clause of the earn-out agreement.
In this regard, the claimants would argue otherwise.
The claimants would, first of all, highlight to the
arbitrator that the arbitrator being the competent
authority approved and jointly appointed by the parties
in the arbitration clause of the earn-out agreement, and
complying with the principle of competence-competence,
the arbitrator can decide its own jurisdiction,
especially in the context and the facts and the
documentation requires the arbitrator to consider both
disputes, documents and the relevant evidence in this
context.
Not only that, the earn-out agreement expressly
incorporates the design and build termination mechanism.
In this regard, there are multiple clauses in which
there are cross-references and intertwined drafting, or
clauses.  However, for the purposes of current
discussion I would like to highlight clause 3.4, which
says the 3.4 to be applied, the DBC has to be terminated
as per the clause 15.2.
So it makes it very clear that the arbitrator cannot
look at the grounds of EOA in isolation because it
necessitates the arbitrator to look under certain
aspects that falls within the purview or ambit of the
design and build contract.
When you essentially have a case of termination on
grounds that are under the design and construction
agreement, then you cannot ignore that factor and then
just focus on whether the parties are entitled to the
compensation under earn-out agreement.
So, our submission is that because of the
interoperability and because of the compatibility of
these agreements, or because the way in which these
documents are drafted and expected to be interpreted by
the parties, the arbitrator has to look into the aspects
that are to be covered under the design and build
construction contract.
Moreover, the DIAC court has taken a stand while
making observations on the consolidation of both claims
that there is nothing that prevents the arbitrator from
considering evidence under DBC.
So from a point of view of looking into evidence,
facts, and interpretation, even the DIAC court also
acknowledges that the arbitrator would have to utilise
or use that interconnectivity or the elements of
considering aspects in the design and build construction
while looking into or interpreting the earn-out
agreement; and entitlements under earn-out agreement.
Our third point is that the claimants are not
seeking an independent relief under DBC.  If you look at
our submissions, we are not making any claims under the
DBC.  All our claims are under the earn-out agreement.
So, therefore, that is also a position that that doesn't
exclude the arbitrator from looking into documents or
evidence with respect to interpretation or
considerations of DBC.
Last but not least, it is also interesting to note
that the respondents themselves have relied on the DBC
termination clause.
So when, on the one hand, they argue that the
tribunal cannot look into the DBC, the design and build
construction related aspects or grounds, they have
essentially relied on the clauses in the design and
build construction contract to make their counterclaim.
So their counterclaim of liquidated damages, and
their termination of the EOA, both are stemming from
interpretation of the clauses in the design and build
contract.
Therefore, on the basis of these broad points,
I would like to humbly submit that this arbitral
tribunal has the jurisdiction to look into evidence, and
also to look into merits of facts related to design and
build construction contract.
ARBITRATOR:  May I ask you a question?
MS BEJOY:  Yes.
ARBITRATOR:  Can you a little bit more elaborate on the
point which you just raised about the DIAC court?
I couldn't get your point.
MS BEJOY:  Yes, arbitrator.
In this regard, I would like to refer to --
ARBITRATOR:  Apologies I'm just trying to clarify some
points on your submissions.  I like to address some
things within the time you are explaining your cases,
okay, so I'm sorry I'm interrupting your thought, but
I have to do it this way.
MS BEJOY:  Not at all, arbitrator.  I'm pleased to assist
you.
Learned arbitrator, if I may ask, what is the
clarification that you are seeking?
ARBITRATOR:  You just talked about, if I'm not mistaking on
your statement, about a DIAC court.
MS BEJOY:  Yes.
ARBITRATOR:  And their finding, or their observation about
the second agreements, right?
ARBITRATOR:  So can you a little bit elaborate?  I couldn't
get your point here.
MS BEJOY:  Learned arbitrator, to give you background,
basically the claimants have filed two claims.  There is
a claim number 27 -- the current claim which is filed
under the earn-out agreement, and there was also another
claim which was filed under the design and build
construction contract.
ARBITRATOR:  Yes, I know that, yes.
MS BEJOY:  So what happened is later they have decided to
withdraw their claim related to the design and build
construction contract when they realised that their
request --
ARBITRATOR:  You guys decided?
MS BEJOY:  Yes, because we requested for a consolidation.
ARBITRATOR:  The claimants?
MS BEJOY:  Yes, as a claimant.  Which then did not happen
because the DIAC court came with the view that there is
no consolidation possible in the current case because
the arbitration clause in the agreements are different.
And the parties are also different.
So what happened was we withdrew the claim filed
under the design and build construction contract, and we
decided to proceed under the earn-out agreement
arbitration clause.
However, the DIAC, in its reply, highlighted that
there is nothing that prevents the arbitrator from
relying on DBC-related submissions as a matter of
evidence in deciding the earn-out agreement.  If you
just give me one minute, I will pull out the relevant
documentation.
ARBITRATOR:  Mm-hmm.
MS BEJOY:  So my submission is, I would say, two levels of
submission in that.  See, that was very early in the
stage of the proceeding, when the DIAC has made this
observation.  It is also my view that DIAC has made that
observation in its administrative capacity.
Thirdly, although their preliminary view is that the
agreements are not compatible because of difference in
the arbitration clause, our submission is that it is
compatible because the underlying dispute is the same,
the project is the same.  Although there are two
documents.  Both are dealing with the same project,
which is the development of Yotel project.
It is admitted that there are additional parties in
the design and build construction contract.  However, if
we apply the test, the mere fact that the project
related to both the contracts is the same, it is my
submission that although the administrative view of DIAC
is that it cannot be consolidated, I feel and my view is
that as a learned arbitrator you have every right to
look into these two contracts.
Why do I say so?  More so from a practical point of
view also.  Because if we look at the way these
contracts are drafted, design and build construction
contract does not talk about any benefits.  Design and
build construction contract is only about obligations of
the parties in terms of performing the construction
contract.  Whereas if that is achieved, then the relief
or the results or the return lies in the earn-out
agreement.
So one cannot look into one document and come to
a final or conclusion for a dispute because that would
essentially lead the parties to a very prejudicial
position, and would also lead to multiplicity of
proceeding.  Because today we have a dispute under
earn-out agreement.  Tomorrow, if we have another
dispute under the design and build construction, we are
talking about multiple forums, multiple arbitrator
tribunal all coming with different views.
So how would practically that affect the parties?
So considering all of this, it is my humble submission
that now that the parties have invested more than a year
in this dispute, and a lot of evidence has come in from
both parties, both in terms of the earn-out agreement
and the design and build construction agreement, both
should be looked into as one part and parcel, because
the underlying dispute, or the project related to the
dispute is one and the same.
ARBITRATOR:  I got your point.  But I have another question
also related to that.  I understand your point related
to the practicality and the interlink between both the
agreements, but can you address it more about the
legality of different parties -- there is one party
missing on this arbitration.  What do you think about it
in this regard?  Because you are talking about
practical.  I am a tribunal sitting here, I have to look
at the legality first, before practical, right?
What do you think about it?  There is one party that
is not available here.  Is it right for me to look at it
while one party is missing?
MS BEJOY:  Yes, I agree with you, arbitrator, that yes, if
one party is missing in a proceeding, and if they are
essentially a party to the contract, that would
definitely lead to a position where that party will be
denied of a fair opportunity to present their case.
Can we look at the current scenario, because who are
the parties to the current contract.  If I may please
take your learned arbitrator to the underlying
documents, we have, first, the earn-out agreement --
let's start with the MOU.  I think MOU is, I think, on
page -- it is {D44} is MOU.
So we have in the MOU --
ARBITRATOR:  Can you please put it up?  Enlarge it a little
bit.  Thank you.  Go ahead.
MS BEJOY:  So the parties to the MOU is Pacific Real Estate
Development LLC, which is claimant 1 in the current
proceeding.  We have IFA Hotels and Resorts FZE, which
is respondent number 2 in the current proceeding, and we
have Balquis Residence FZE LLC, which is respondent 1 in
the current proceeding.  So those are the parties to the
memorandum of understanding.
If we move on to the next document, that is the
earn-out agreement, that's {D5}, so if you look at the
parties to the earn-out agreement, we have Pacific,
again, claimant 1.  Ayad -- Mr Alhabshi, he is very much
present and he is also claimant number 3 in the current
proceeding.  Then he have Turfa Building, which is
claimant 2 in the current proceeding, and then we have
Balquis and IFA hotels.
So all of the parties are very much present.
If we move on and look at the design and build
contract, which is {D50}, the parties to the dispute
again are Balquis, which is respondent number 1 in the
current proceeding, and Turfa, which is claimant
number 2 in the current proceeding.
So there is no third party in any of these
contracts.  However, if you look at earn-out agreement
and the design and build construction contract, we have
Pacific missing in the design and construction contract.
However, in the current proceeding, Pacific is
claimant number 1 and the sole beneficiary for the
obligations under the design and build construction
contract.
If I'm not wrong, there are also some
cross-guarantees given by Pacific and Balquis.  So
basically, to explain to you, arbitrator, Pacific is the
holding company, or the investment company, and Turfa is
the construction counsel.
So in the earn-out, parties purposefully did not --
sorry, the earn-out agreement was drafted in such a way
that Pacific will have the benefit, provided Turfa
performs under the design and build construction
contract.  So that is the interconnectivity with both
contracts.
Also could be because construction contract requires
construction capabilities and other details which was
not pretty much the focus of Pacific.  Pacific is a real
estate company.  I'll be taking arbitrator through the
trade licences of the entities to show why there is
relevance for certain party to be reflected, names to be
reflected in a certain document.
ARBITRATOR:  Sure.
MS BEJOY:  Yes.  So my submission is that if you look at the
parties participated in the proceeding, in today's
proceeding, it is very unlikely that a party will have
a claim that they have been not heard or they have been
prejudiced, because the arbitrator has combined both
agreements and related merits to today's proceeding.
Because this proceeding has everybody on board, and
through the process of the arbitration, we have had
evidences flowing in related to Pacific, related to
Turfa, related to Balquis, related to IFA, so everybody
has been given ample opportunity to present their side
of the case.  And it is only fair that, to the parties,
again, because if we have to initiate one more
proceeding, we are talking about another arbitral
tribunal and whether advance on cost, another one or two
years to be spent in the proceeding all for coming to
a conclusion which could be completely opposite to or
conflicting with the current tribunal's decision.  And
when it comes to the enforceability point, how would it
affect the parties, and where is the efficiency of the
arbitration proceeding for which the parties have opted
in for arbitration?
ARBITRATOR:  May I go to the arbitration clause in both
agreements?
MS BEJOY:  Yes.
ARBITRATOR:  Design and build and the earn-out.  Can you
just put both of them together?  Sorry, I'm taking from
your time, I know that.
MS BEJOY:  Much obliged, arbitrator.
ARBITRATOR:  Can we put arbitration clause for both
agreements?
MS BEJOY:  For the first document it is inside page 9,
earn-out agreement.  You can go to page {D5-9}.
For the design and build it is internal page.
MR LIXENBURG:  {D50-92}.
MS BEJOY:  Yes, thank you.
ARBITRATOR:  That's okay. {D50-92}.
Read both clauses.
MS BEJOY:  Yes.
ARBITRATOR:  The difference between both of them -- both of
them is the arbitration -- but you cannot sit that on
design and build, there is a condition required on the
arbitrator.
MS BEJOY:  Yes.
ARBITRATOR:  So what is your opinion about the difference
here?
Here the parties agreed that there is some
qualification on the arbitrator, which is not on me.
That's clear.  Right?
MS BEJOY:  Yes.
ARBITRATOR:  So what is your opinion about the difference
here.  There is two agreements, two different things.
Okay?  Two different clauses.  So what do you think?
MS BEJOY:  I do understand there are certain specifications
regarding the qualifications of the arbitrator in the
design and build construction contract.  However,
I would be approaching this in a very practical view,
learned arbitrator, because when we filed the claim
under the earn-out agreement, what could have triggered
the parties to consider that certain specific qualities
should be there for the arbitrator?  It could be because
DBC is a construction contract, so the construction
requires specialised knowledge so that it is very
technical sometimes in nature.
So just to address the complexity of the dispute,
the parties then thought it would be better to have
a more technically qualified person to sit as an
arbitrator in a construction dispute.
However, if you look at the nature of the dispute
that we are currently looking at under the earn-out
agreement, that also requires the arbitrator to apply
those types of skills because in order to arrive at the
conclusion of the earn-out agreement, the underlying
project is a construction project.  The contract that is
leading up to the termination is again construction in
nature.  Plus, the parties have elected to have you as
the learned arbitrator in the earn-out agreement.
The parties also had the whole list of experts
assisting them and assisting you, learned arbitrator, in
resolving and navigating any technical issues that you
may come across in deciding the claims raised by the
parties under the earn-out agreement.
So while I would like to address this in detail,
maybe perhaps after a break, however, my preliminary
view is that just because there is an added
qualification requirement under the design and build
construction contract, by taking a pro arbitration
approach, by consolidating contracts that are having
same underlying project, and that are having multiple
clauses that are cross-referred, arbitrator should
assume jurisdiction, or rather there is jurisdiction
under the current disputes to hear matters pertaining to
design and build construction contract.
Also, arbitrator, I would like to just produce the
document that you have been previously requesting me,
that is {E137}.  The observation from the DIAC.
So, learned arbitrator, if you may look at this,
this is an email address to Mr Alhabshi and DIAC is
saying:
"As set out in the previous email, the claims under
the two contracts proceed separately and therefore only
claims arising from the Earn Out Agreement can be
pursued as case 240007 following the Court's decision on
consolidation (subject to ..."
That's more important, learned arbitrator:
" ... any further decision made by the Tribunal)."
So the DIAC is leaving it to your hands to decide
whether you can take a different view when it comes to
consolidation of both disputes.
Just a minor point that I would like to add on.  The
claimants would like to clarify, and make it clear that
all our claims in the current dispute is only pertaining
to reliefs that are secured under the earn-out
agreement.  What we are requesting the arbitrator is to
consider evidence or factual merits that are pertaining
to the design and build construction contract.
Because, see, the problem is we have two contracts,
and there is a lot of interconnected clauses.
In order to decide and in order to do justice to
returns under the earn-out agreement, it is impossible
to make a decision under earn-out agreement without
looking into what was the obligations of the parties
under the design and build construction contract.
Typically, to give you an example, learned
arbitrator, one of the grounds taken by them is that the
claimants did not meet the expected standards or did not
produce designs.  So where is that requirement coming
from?  There is no requirement under earn-out agreement.
So the requirement for earn-out, the design is only
under design and construction contract.  And one of the
grounds taken by them determinate the earn-out agreement
and the design and construction contract is lack of
producing designs, lack of producing consultants and
employees, certifications.
Thirdly, the financing.
Of course, the financing may have overarching effect
under the earn-out agreement.  But if you look at the
other two other grounds that are firmly rooted under
obligations that are coming from the design and build
construction contract, and they want the learned
arbitrator to make a decision that their termination is
valid.
So how would the learned arbitrator come to that
conclusion without looking into the clauses of the
design and build construction contract, without looking
into merits, evidence and documents produced by the
parties with respect to the design and build
construction contract?
So that is the situation that we are in.
And more so, if I may please take your arbitrator to
clause 3.4, which is a very important clause for today's
discussions of the earn-out agreement, page number
It reads:
"In the event that the Construction Contract [which
is the design and build contract] is terminated
following issue of a notice of termination by Balquis
under Clause 15.2 ..."
15.2 of which contract?  Of the design and build
construction contract:
" ... thereof Balquis shall be entitled to terminate
this Earn-Out Agreement immediately upon written notice
to [Pacific] and the sole liability of Balquis to PRED
(whether under this Earn-Out Agreement or otherwise at
law) shall be for the amount due as calculated in
accordance with Clause 3.5 of this Earn-Out Agreement."
So it is their position that they have served
a valid notice under 15.2, of correction notice under
15.2 of the design and build construction contract which
is very much into clause 3.4 of the earn-out agreement.
So in order to decide on the entitlement of the
parties under 3.4, arbitrator would have to look into
the legality or the maintainability of the notice of
correction issued under DBC.
ARBITRATOR:  Okay.  I notice much of your statement is based
on the practicality, which is understandable.  But can
you support what you are talking about in case law, the
law itself?  Because you are -- practical is something
what we are on the case here.  We have to have -- you
need to show me what is your ground legally from the
case law, and you can put this note for the future,
maybe in your submissions, but to substantiate it
legally first, before we get to practical.
MS BEJOY:  Absolutely, sir, if I may please take your
permission, because I do have a note prepared in that
regard, and I will be clarifying this either today
later, in today's submission, or in my closing
submissions.
ARBITRATOR:  Sure.  Please go ahead then.
MS BEJOY:  Thank you very much.
I would like to now move on to my second preliminary
issue, that is regarding the counterclaim submitted by
the respondents.
So we understand that the respondents would like to
pursue a counterclaim for 16 million dirhams and
incidentally, we have received a notification from Dubai
Arbitration Centre yesterday or the day before yesterday
that they are yet to formally register the counterclaim
with the DIAC.
As per the DIAC Rules, if a counterclaim is not
formally registered, it is a mandatory requirement, then
the tribunal cannot look into the counterclaim
^word    proffered by the parties.
In that regard, I have also extracted the
relevant -- but, of course, you know, I understand that
DIAC has given them time until 18 -- three/four days for
them to file, register the counterclaim, so I would not
want to make any submissions with respect to that,
because my submission is that as of now there is no
registered counterclaim with DIAC, and DIAC has already
acknowledged it in their yesterday's communication.
Second level of challenge on the counterclaim is
that the counterclaim is coming after the limitation
period.
ARBITRATOR:  So do you want to make a submission on their
counterclaim or you don't want to do it?
MS BEJOY:  We don't want to.  My submission is that the
arbitrator should not entertain the counterclaim because
they have not essentially registered a counterclaim, not
met with the administrative requirement of paying the
relevant fee --
ARBITRATOR:  That's administration.  It is up to you whether
you want to address it or not.  Because this is your
chance to do it.  If you don't want it, it is up to you.
MS BEJOY:  Yes, so without prejudice I would like to submit
to you, sir, that yes, there are administrative lacunas.
And the second point is, this counterclaim, if they are
pursuing it, my second level of submission is that it is
coming after the limitation period.  The limitation
period in this case is six years.  The governing law, as
per the current contract, is the DIAC laws, and as per
DIAC law the limitation period is six years, and the
limitation period should start from 18 January 2018,
when they terminated the contract, which would end on
17 January 2024.
So we have almost passed two years after the
limitation period, and therefore, my submission on
a without prejudice basis is that even if they rectified
the administrative lacuna, it should not be entertained
because it is coming after substantial delay from the
limitation period.
So those were my two preliminary issues.
With your kind permission, learned arbitrator, if
I may please move on to the next segment of my
submission, that is key background information.
I would like to touch upon a few things that has
come to the claimants' notice from the beginning of the
case which are very important and relevant and which
should be understood in a proper way in order to
understand the case of both parties.
The first one that I would like to talk about is the
issue of financing, and the respondents' financial
constraints.
In this regard, I would like your learned arbitrator
to please refer to the annual financial reports
submitted by them, more precisely the AFR of -- I'll
